name: Modern Farmhouse

geography.hearth: No design hearth. Its transmission hearth is Waco, Texas, by way of television and a retail brand, and its production hearth is the Sun Belt builder market.

lineage.note: Silhouette only, and this edge is deliberately typed as a reference rather than a descent. What is quoted is the outline: a simple steep gable, vertical boarding, a metal roof, a porch. What is not transmitted is everything that made the original work — the 10:12 to 12:12 pitch, the 12-to-18-inch overhang with a moulded rake return, the full-depth working porch, the small openings in a thick wall, and the accretive plan that grew by ells over generations.
The economy, and the specific habit of deleting the overhang first. The lineage of cost engineering runs unbroken from the 1936 FHA bulletin to a 2020 elevation with a 6-inch rake.

The apparatus: production builders, elevation packages, engineered trusses, sheet-goods modules, the 9-to-10-foot plate, and the street-facing garage. Structurally this is a neo-eclectic house with a different skin.

And at the same time a genuine reaction against it: monochrome instead of contrasting materials, one grammar instead of six, simple gables instead of stacked ones, restraint instead of accumulation. Both edges are true, which is the most interesting fact about this node.
The plan and the section: open great room, island kitchen, indoor-outdoor rear relationship, attached garage on the frontage.

description.short: The market-dominant American idiom of the 2010s and 2020s: white board-and-batten or lap siding with black windows and black metal accents under a simple gable, descending in silhouette from the farmhouse vernacular, in economy from minimal traditional, in apparatus from the production builder, and in section from contemporary open planning.
description.long:
Modern Farmhouse is the first traditional idiom selected by photograph. Its predecessors were transmitted by pattern book, magazine, catalog, or code — media that carry plans, sections, and dimensions. This one was transmitted by television and by image feeds: HGTV's Fixer Upper ran from 2013 to 2018 out of Waco, Texas, and the Magnolia brand that grew from it converted a renovation aesthetic into a national exterior style; Pinterest and Instagram did the rest. That transmission medium has a specific consequence which explains nearly every characteristic of the style: an image at thumbnail size carries value contrast and silhouette and carries nothing at all of profile depth, reveal, or shadow. So the style optimizes hard for the first two and abandons the third. White wall, black window, black roof, simple outline: it is extremely legible on a screen, and it is thin in front of you.

The material and technical conditions are as specific as the media ones. Fibre-cement board-and-batten and lap siding — Hardie, LP SmartSide — made a durable, paintable, dead-flat vertical wall available in four-by-eight and four-by-ten panels at production-builder prices; this is the actual enabler, and it is why the wall is flat, because the panel is. Black-clad aluminium and vinyl windows fell in price in the 2010s and became a stock item rather than an upcharge. Standing-seam metal, formerly agricultural and industrial, became a residential accent product. Meanwhile the open great room with an island kitchen pushed the ground-floor plate to nine and often ten feet, which raised the window head to eight feet, which left one to two feet of blank wall between head and soffit — a gap the historical farmhouse never had, because its heads died into the frieze within six to ten inches. The garage remained where the ranch left it, on the street.

Where it characteristically fails is worth stating precisely, because these are five measurable deviations from the thing it quotes, and correcting them would cost very little. Roof pitch: the vernacular farmhouse gable runs 10:12 to 12:12; the market version flattens to 6:12 or 8:12 to reduce truss cost and attic volume, and the result reads as a shed with a tall wall rather than a house under a roof. Overhang: the historical eave projected twelve to eighteen inches with a moulded rake and a cornice return at the gable corner; the market version boxes it at zero to eight inches, so the wall meets the sky at a knife edge, the gable never terminates, and no part of the wall is ever in shadow. Window head height: heads set by the plate rather than by the wall composition, leaving twelve to twenty-four inches of blank siding above them and misaligning heads between storeys. Porch: reduced from a full-width working porch of eight to ten feet to an entry shed of five or six, which is a gesture rather than a room and is never furnished. And contrast substituting for depth: black on white is being asked to do the work that three to six inches of projection used to do. It photographs beautifully and, at twenty feet, produces a house made entirely of outline.

The fair assessment is that this is the closest thing to a shared national traditional idiom since the ranch, and that it is a real improvement on what it replaced. It is restrained, it is coherent, it uses one grammar per building, and it has largely stopped applying half-width shutters and three-material fronts. Its interiors are genuinely good — light from two or three sides, generous circulation, an intelligible plan. The deficiency is precisely five dimensions deep: pitch, eave overhang, rake overhang, head-to-soffit distance, and porch depth. Fix those five and the idiom becomes a good style rather than a photographed one — which is a nearly perfect demonstration of what a small, enforceable, numeric rule set can be worth, and the reason this node is included in a design system rather than merely described in a field guide.

defining_characteristics: Simple dominant gable forms with minimal cross-gabling and a legible single roof hierarchy
Vertical board-and-batten or narrow lap siding, or the two combined by storey, in a single light value
High-contrast dark window frames, trim, and roof accents against a light wall — a strict two-value palette
Standing-seam metal roofing at porches, dormers, or the whole roof
A covered entry or partial porch under a shed or extended gable roof
Open great-room plan with a 9 to 10 ft ground-floor plate and correspondingly high window heads
Ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements, no material changes at an outside corner
diagnostic_tells: Black windows in a white wall, with no trim colour in between
Board-and-batten to the gable or upper storey over lap siding below, with the change occurring at a floor line
A standing-seam shed roof over the entry, in a different plane and material from the main roof
Overhangs under 12 in, boxed, with no rake return at the gable corner
Gooseneck barn lights over the garage doors and a sliding barn door somewhere visible through the glazing

distinguished_from.difference: The original has a steeper roof (10:12-12:12), a real eave and rake overhang with a cornice return, small openings in proportion to solid wall, a full-width porch of habitable depth, and an accreted plan of ells built over decades. The modern version has one mass, a flat eave, a high plate, and a shed porch. Almost every difference is measurable.

Simplification versus accumulation. Neo-eclectic multiplies gables, materials, window shapes, and quoted motifs; modern farmhouse reduces to one gable family, one material, one window type, and no motifs. Both are production-builder products with the same plans behind them.

A look versus a code. New Urbanist towns frequently build in this idiom, and when they do the code forces the porch depth, the pitch, and the garage relegation — which produces a visibly better version of the same style and demonstrates that the failures listed here are enforcement failures, not stylistic ones.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Photographic and economic. The operative modules are the fibre-cement panel (4 x 8 and 4 x 10 ft), the 24-inch truss, the 9-to-10-foot plate, and the 16- or 18-foot garage door. Composition proceeds by silhouette and colour value rather than by profile and shadow, and that single substitution is what separates the idiom from every style it quotes. Recording the as-built and the source dimensions side by side, as below, is the most useful thing this node can carry.
typical_ratios: Principal gable pitch as built 6:12 to 8:12; vernacular source 10:12 to 12:12
Eave and rake overhang as built 0 to 8 in; vernacular source 12 to 18 in with a cornice return
Window head to soffit or frieze as built 12 to 24 in; vernacular source 6 to 10 in
Window opening proportion 1:1.7 to 1:2.0, commonly ganged in twos and threes
Ground plate 9 to 10 ft; window head 8 ft 0 in
Entry porch depth as built 5 to 6 ft; vernacular source 8 to 10 ft full width
Wall-to-trim luminance contrast greater than 8:1, doing the work of profile depth
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular ganged openings at 8 to 14 ft centres on the principal elevation, with the garage terminating one end; heads generally aligned within a storey, which is a genuine advance over the preceding node.

massing_affinities.note: The quoted skeleton, and the one the idiom handles best because the ell gives a secondary mass without requiring a stacked gable.
The single-storey market version, particularly in the Sun Belt.
Works surprisingly well, because a hipped or steep-gabled square mass tolerates the flat wall and the high plate better than a long elevation does.

constraints.statement: Principal gable pitch not less than 6:12, and 10:12 preferred. Below 8:12 the mass reads as a shed and the quoted vernacular silhouette is lost.

test.note: Tests the hard 6:12 floor. '10:12 preferred' and 'below 8:12 reads as a shed' are softer descriptive guidance beyond the hard floor and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Rake overhang not less than 8 in and eave overhang not less than 12 in, with a returned or moulded termination at every gable corner. Zero-overhang boxed rakes are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the eave-overhang floor. Rake overhang (8in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose -- no vocabulary variable distinctly expresses rake-overhang projection depth (rake_trim_width_in is the rake trim board's face width, a different measurement). The returned/moulded gable-corner termination is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window heads shall sit not more than 10 in below the soffit or frieze line, and shall align to one datum per storey. Where the plate exceeds 9 ft, either raise the head or introduce a transom to close the gap.

test.note: Tests the head-to-soffit/frieze offset ceiling. 'Align to one datum per storey' has no vocabulary variable for same-storey cross-elevation head alignment (opening_vertical_alignment_in is storey-to-storey, a different comparison) and stays prose, as does the plate-exceeds-9ft transom clause.

constraints.statement: Board-and-batten battens at 16 or 24 in on centre aligned to the framing, minimum 1x2 nominal with not less than 3/4 in projection. Battens at 12 in centres or with projection under 1/2 in read as stripes rather than as boarding.
A covered space may be described as a porch only at 8 ft or more of clear depth across not less than 40 percent of the facade. Shallower entry roofs are hoods and must be detailed as such.

test.note: Tests the clear-depth floor. The 40-percent-of-facade-width clause has no matching porch-width variable (gallery_depth_ft is depth only) and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Fixer Upper renovations
exemplars.note: The 2013-2018 television series and the Magnolia brand that followed. Listed as the style's transmission event rather than as architectural authorship, because that is honestly what it is: the idiom has no canonical designed building, and saying so is more useful than inventing one.

exemplars.name: Serenbe, Selborne hamlet
exemplars.note: Steve Nygren's New Urbanist community, first houses sold 2005 and built out since. The same farmhouse idiom under a form-based code that enforces porch depth, setback, and garage relegation — the control case showing what the style looks like when the five failing dimensions are regulated.

sources: Thomas C. Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England (1984)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Marianne Cusato and Brent Hull, Get Your House Right: Architectural Elements to Use and Avoid (2007)
Dolores Hayden, Building Suburbia: Green Fields and Urban Growth, 1820-2000 (2003)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. The node's defining_characteristics ('Simple dominant gable forms with minimal cross-gabling and a legible single roof hierarchy') is this pack's dominance rule intact, and its canonical massing (linear-ell-farmhouse -- 'the ell gives a secondary mass without requiring a stacked gable') is a dominant-block-plus-subordinate-ell composition of exactly the kind this pack's wing_strategy and dominance rules describe. Bound primary/facade with the deviation stated plainly, because the node itself states it with unusual precision -- pitch as built 6:12-8:12 against the pack's picturesque-vernacular expectation and the node's own named 10:12-12:12 source; eave as built 0-8 in against this pack's own default eave projection of about 21 in; window head as built 12-24 in below soffit against a 6-10 in vernacular source. This is the same relationship this pack has to american-farmhouse-vernacular one link up the lineage, except here the node's own long description supplies the deviation table itself ('Recording the as-built and the source dimensions side by side... is the most useful thing this node can carry'), so the binding is confirmed by the node's own text rather than merely inferred.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to, and a materially closer fit here than on its ancestor american-farmhouse-vernacular (where it is bound optional and only for the 1900-1920 tail). Constraint c04 -- board-and-batten battens at 16 or 24 in on centre aligned to the framing, minimum 1x2 nominal, not less than 3/4 in projection -- is this pack's flat-stock, board-series logic almost exactly: a batten sized against the framing module is precisely how this pack's whole family is generated ('the base is a one-by-eight because a one-by-eight is a board'). Unlike american-farmhouse-vernacular, this node has no surviving classical-order-derived trim tradition competing with it -- defining_characteristics state 'ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements, no material changes at an outside corner' -- so this is the primary and effectively only trim system genuinely present, bound at role interior (this schema's slot for a governing trim family) rather than optional.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes say what it is: Gibbs's Ionic order as a delta on Vignola -- an entablature at one fifth of the column, three fasciae, modillions at three quarters of a diameter, a pedestal rule. It is a classical order, and on this node it is governing `pilaster` and `door_surround`, which are applied classical elements in the literal sense. The node's defining_characteristics state flatly that applied classical elements are absent, and the node's own author already reasoned from that same sentence when binding `trim-craftsman`, writing that this node has no surviving classical-order-derived trim tradition competing with it. This is not the blanket-refusal trap: the record does not merely say 'no proportional system', it names the exact class of thing this pack supplies and says the style does not carry it.
declined_packs.quote: Ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements
declined_packs.note: Governs 4 slots: casing, cornice, door_surround, pilaster. Declining reassigns all four and strands none -- casing falls to palladio-tuscan (italian-renaissance); cornice, door_surround and pilaster fall to chambers-ionic (english-georgian). 0 slots lose all dimensioning. Note that the replacements are themselves classical orders, so this decline removes a wrong authority without supplying a right one (OQ 58's stated limit); the successor packs are separate gaps for separate adjudication. --pair reports that ENDORSING would arm build/elevation.py::gibbs_applies; a decline arms nothing.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's notes describe the Gibbs Doric order: an Attic base, scrolled modillions replacing mutules, a triglyph-and-metope frieze with square metopes three quarters of a diameter on a side, twenty-four semicircular flutes. That is an applied classical order, and the same sentence in the node's defining_characteristics that refuses applied classical elements refuses it. The node reinforces this where it distinguishes itself from neo-eclectic -- it reduces to one gable family, one material, one window type, and no motifs -- and its long description records that the idiom has largely stopped applying half-width shutters and three-material fronts. A pediment dimensioned off a Doric triglyph frieze is a motif this record says the style does not carry.
declined_packs.quote: Ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements
declined_packs.note: Governs 1 slot: pediment. Declining reassigns it to facade-classical (colonial-revival); 0 slots lose all dimensioning. As with gibbs-ionic the successor is itself a classical system, so the decline stops this authority without settling the slot -- facade-classical's reach over this node is a separate question.
